en: Then there was the illustrious and most excellent teacher, a noble-born man of refined character,
who knew the truth of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and was devoted to the teachings of Śiva.

One who knows the reality of the objects of knowledge as they have been described, who performs sacrifices, has conquered his senses, is patient yet free from arrogance, and is compassionate toward all living beings; || 2 ||
Faithful, pure, skillful, consecrated by the three initiations, and wise,
he was the one who brought fear and fearlessness, and caused opposition, among gods, asuras, and humans.
Neither deficient in limb nor possessing an extra limb, he was endowed with auspicious marks;
he was a knower of place, time, and omens, and the most excellent among those who understand locations, lands, and complexions.

He should be knowledgeable in the lunar days, constellations, and astrological conjunctions; skilled in the rite of seizing the ground; an expert in the specific requirements of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa); and proficient in the Śiva-maṇḍala.
He is one who knows the scriptures, the qualifications, and the ritual acts, as well as the rules for their subsequent performance;
he is skilled in the rites of the six paths and supreme in the procedure for the Caṇḍayāga sacrifice.
He is one who knows the procedure for consecration, who understands the worship of the site and the concluding rites;
he is a master of yoga, beyond the reach of vows, and learned in the scriptures concerning the rules of transcendence.
He was an expert in the ritual for immediate departure [from the body], skillful in rites for Śiva,
and likewise proficient in mental worship as well as the rules for the water-pot.
Endowed with these very qualities, the wise man, committed to the observance of his duties,
should be constantly non-violent, compassionate, vigilant, and well-supported by companions.

One whose mind is dedicated to the mantra to be accomplished, who is established in the vow of that mantra to be accomplished, and who has been consecrated with that mantra to be accomplished, is proclaimed as a *sādhaka*. 10.
He who has emerged from the three stages of the path, who worships Śiva, the fire, and the guru, and who is established in the mantra and tantra, is known as a *putraka*. 11.
Trembling with fear of the suffering of saṃsāra, his mind fixed on the abode of Śiva, he has reached the hand of Śiva and is a worshiper of Śiva, the fire, and the guru. 12.

Dependent on the guru and lacking independence in all matters at all times, the person who abides by the rules (samayin) is authorized in the scripture while remaining established in the observance (samaya). || 13 ||
The superiority of those with peaceful minds should be understood by those who rely on the knowledge of the leaves, according to the very sequence described in the characteristics. 14.

These [beings], whose forms are unperceived and who have arrived from afar, are to be understood according to their true nature through conventions, just as those meanings of the scriptures [are understood]. 15.
Having approached their guide, purified and composed, those wise ones stood before him, desiring to perform worship. || 16 ||
Then, having seen them, the teacher should resort to the mudrā of the liṅga;
he should mentally contemplate Īśāna, the desired seat of the virtuous. || 17 ||
Having honored the teacher and remaining established in the teacher's observance, O Lord, one should sit to his north upon the "hare-ear" (śaśakarṇikā) [seat]. 18.
Having first formed the *mukulinī* mudrā, the wise practitioner should then slowly place the three digits of Īśāna near the two ears from within the full-blown interior of the lotus.
The other, however, gave the remaining two parts to the preceptor;
likewise addressed, those two touched his hands with their own hands.
Three others should indeed utter three words of the first [name];
then, having uttered the fourth word, he should raise up those who are prostrate.
Having consoled them with words, he should speak these words slowly:
"Speak, O you who know the limits of time and have taken refuge in the path of Śiva."
Now, one should utterly avoid censuring Śiva, Agni, and the Guru, as well as the practitioner, the teacher, the scriptures, and any other person who has received initiation. (23)
One should avoid food touched by a woman who has recently given birth, food offered to the deceased, and the remnants of a funeral meal;
likewise, one should refrain from stepping over flower offerings, giving gifts [to the unworthy], and eating [impure food]. 24.
In this regard, one who stands on the path of Śiva, even if he has attained great power, should not practice the "non-floating" gift toward an animal that lacks discipline. || 25 ||
Thus one should observe these rules of conduct (samayas) as taught by Śiva;
through their observance one attains the state of Śiva, but otherwise one becomes a flesh-eater (kravyāda). 26.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on the General and the Particular, in the Svāyambhuva-sūtra-saṅgraha.
